meaning: The avatāra yet to come — the tenth and final avatāra of Viṣṇu, who appears at the end of the Kali Yuga riding a white horse to destroy unrighteousness and restore the age of truth

phonemes.desc: Conventionally written Kalki; the name is usually derived from kalikā “white horse” or from Kali, the age he ends.
The tenth avatāra of Vishnu, yet to come — the only future god in the lexicon.

kin.label: the
kin.form: White Horse of the world’s end

pronunciation.note: A prophecy made flesh in text: the god who has not yet been born, scheduled for the end of the Kali Yuga.

domains.title: The Tenth Avatāra, the End of the Kali Yuga
domains.subtitle: The Rider Who Comes at the World’s End
domains.lead: Kalki is Vishnu’s final descent: the warrior on the white horse who will come when the Kali Yuga chokes on its own corruption — sword drawn, comet-marked, born in a village to a Brahmin named Viṣṇuyaśas — to end the age, punish the wicked, and restart the world’s golden wheel. He is the only deity in this pantheon whose myth is a prophecy.

cards.name: The White Horse
cards.desc: Devadatta, the winged white steed, given by Śiva; Kalki rides from Śambhala at the age’s end.

cards.name: The Sword of the Age
cards.desc: Ratnamaru, the jewelled sword, given by the gods — it ends the Kali Yuga as a blade ends a lie.

cards.name: Born in Śambhala
cards.desc: His village, Śambhala, waits hidden; when dharma’s four legs shrink to one, he is born there.

cards.name: The Restarter of Time
cards.desc: After the sword, the restart: Kalki inaugurates the next Kṛta Yuga — death midwifing rebirth.

mythology.lead: The Kalki myth is the Purāṇic eschaton: the prophecies of the Kali Yuga’s decay — merchants as kings, wealth as virtue, fathers feared by sons — are the diagnosis, and Kalki is the cure. He appears in the latest strata of the Mahābhārata and the Purāṇas as the tenth and final avatāra, the one Vishnu keeps in reserve for the world’s last night.

myths.title: The Prophecy of the Horse
myths.text: The earliest Kalki-passage names the signs: when time decays, a being of immense power will be born to a family of Brahmins, swift as thought, his hand a sword, his steed white as milk, blazing like a comet. The passage is embedded in the epic’s cosmological books as Vishnu’s promise to the tormented earth.

myths.title: The Full Biography
myths.text: The eponymous Purāṇa tells it whole: the child Kalki, mocked by the corrupt, learns the Vedas from Paraśurāma himself, marries the princess Padmāvatī by the sword-contest, and rides out against the mleccha kings. His campaigns purify the world; the wicked fall to his blade and the earth’s burden lifts at last.

myths.title: The Diagnosis of the Age
myths.text: The Purāṇic Kali-Yuga lists read like satire: rulers will be thieves, vows will be sold, the low will govern the high. Kalki is the answer to this audit — not a reformer but an ending. The theology is cyclical: he destroys the age as a farmer burns the stubble, so the next golden age can be sown.

myths.title: The Expected One
myths.text: Kalki remains expected: in Śambhala-legend — Tibetan Buddhism adopted the hidden kingdom wholesale — and in popular Hinduism, where every generation finds the Kali Yuga’s signs fulfilled. He is the only god in this pantheon whose temple is the future, and whose devotees wait rather than celebrate.

lore.syncretism: The Kalki cycle absorbed apocalyptic expectations from every quarter: the White Horse echoes the sun-horse of Indo-Iranian myth; the sword of the age borrows Paraśurāma’s axe; and Śambhala, his hidden kingdom, became the axis of Tibetan Buddhism’s Kalacakra — the wheel of time teachings centred on the king who will come.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kalki is eschatology’s most durable prophetic figure in the living world: films, novels, and comics re-stage his coming endlessly, and ‘waiting for Kalki’ is an idiom for expecting the end of a corrupt order. The Śambhala legend seeded Theosophy’s Shambhala and, through it, a century of Western occult geography.
lore.extendedMeditation: Kalki: a name that is a countdown. Restored plainly, it stands at the lexicon’s far edge — the god who has no past tense. Every other entry in this temple restores what was; this one restores what will be, and the plain letters are appropriate: the last avatāra needs no decoration on his way to end the age.
lore.archaeology: No ancient Kalki temples — he has not yet been born. But his images ride through South Indian temple friezes of the Dashavatāra, and the Śambhala iconography of Tibetan thangkas gives his myth a monumental afterlife in paint across the Himalayas.
lore.cult: His cult is expectation: the recitation of the Kali-Yuga signs, the keeping of the Dashavatāra sequence with the tenth place left open. In South India, Kalki devotion has produced modern temples — the only god in the lexicon whose shrines post-date his prophecy’s writing.
lore.iconography: A blazing horseman on Devadatta, sword high, often four-armed with bow and discus — Vishnu’s weapons on the rider’s frame. The comet’s tail marks his banner; behind him the armies of the age’s end ride out from Śambhala’s gates.
lore.reception: Comparative eschatology sets Kalki beside the Mahdi, the Maitreya, and the Second Coming as the great expected ones — but unique among them in arriving by prophecy rather than promise. Modern fiction from Gore Vidal’s Kalki to manga has made his name a byword for the terminal avatar.
